Introduction: Pesticide Epidemiology and Categories

Rosen source check

Rosen Table 152.1. Pesticide Classes and Examples

Use this next to the chapter taxonomy before diving into OP/carbamate management.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen groups pesticide classes more broadly and explicitly includes substituted phenols, chlorinated hydrocarbons, glyphosate, and DEET; Tintinalli Table 201-1 is narrower for insecticides/repellents, then separates herbicides/rodenticides later.
Tintinalli source check

Table 201-1. Insecticides and Repellents

Use this table as the taxonomy map for the chapter: OPs, carbamates, organochlorines, pyrethroids, neonicotinoids, nereistoxin analogs, and the key repellent agents.

Pesticides include insecticides, herbicides, and rodenticides that produce toxicity from intentional, accidental, and occupational exposures. More than 150,000 pesticide poisoning deaths occur each year worldwide, with insecticides accounting for the majority of the mortality. Pesticide toxicity results from both active ingredients and formulation components including solvents and surfactants.

Six major classes of insecticides are in common use: organophosphates, carbamates, organochlorines, pyrethrins/pyrethroids, neonicotinoids, and nereistoxin analogs. The World Health Organization classifies pesticides by toxicity based on rodent LD50 values; however, human case-fatality rates display large variation within same toxicity classification.

Exposure Pathways

  • Dermal absorption (especially if skin abraded or with prolonged contact)
  • Inhalation (highest risk with spray applications and volatile formulations)
  • Oral/GI ingestion (accidental or intentional)
  • Transconjunctival absorption (eye contact with aerosols)
  • Mucous membrane contact

Global Epidemiology

  • >150,000 deaths annually from pesticide poisoning worldwide
  • Insecticides responsible for majority of mortality
  • Organophosphate and carbamate compounds most common in healthcare facility attendance in United States
  • Globally, organophosphate poisoning results most commonly from deliberate self-poisoning
  • Accidental exposures occur in agricultural/industrial settings
  • Children at greater risk due to smaller body size and lower baseline cholinesterase levels
  • Farmworkers, pesticide applicators, pet groomers at occupational risk

Management Cornerstone

  • Precise product identification from container label essential (active AND inert ingredients)
  • Consultation with poison control center or medical toxicologist recommended
  • Early identification of exposures amenable to antidotal therapy
  • Meticulous supportive care critical for survival

Organophosphates: Mechanism and Clinical Features

Tintinalli source check

Table 201-2. Clinical Effects of Cholinergic Excess

Place this beside OP clinical features: muscarinic SLUDGE/DUMBELS, nicotinic weakness/fasciculations, and CNS agitation to coma are the board stem backbone.

Rosen source check

Rosen Fig. 152.1. Cholinergic Effects on the Nervous System

This figure maps ACh effects across somatic, parasympathetic, sympathetic, and CNS pathways.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen gives a visual receptor-system map that Tintinalli does not; it explains why OP poisoning can produce both miosis/bronchorrhea and nicotinic tachycardia/HTN/mydriasis.
Rosen source check

Rosen Box 152.1. Cholinergic Toxidrome (SLUDGE DUMBELS)

A compact toxidrome memory box to read beside Tintinalli Table 201-2.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen emphasizes the mnemonic box; Tintinalli adds a clearer split into muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS effects. Use both: mnemonic for recall, Tintinalli for mechanism-based sorting.

Commonly used organophosphates include diazinon, acephate, malathion, parathion, and chlorpyrifos. Organophosphate potency varies: highly potent compounds such as parathion are used in agriculture, whereas intermediate potency agents including coumaphos and trichlorfon are used in animal care. Diazinon and chlorpyrifos were phased out from household use in the United States in 2000 due to neurotoxicity, particularly affecting developing brains of children.

Globally, organophosphate poisoning results most commonly from deliberate self-poisoning. Accidental exposures occur in agricultural and industrial settings through pesticide spray applicators and spills during transport. Inadvertent exposure can occur from flea-dip products in pet groomers and children, and from contaminated food.

Enzyme Targets

  • Organophosphate compounds irreversibly bind and inactivate two forms of cholinesterase:
  • Acetylcholinesterase (true/red blood cell acetylcholinesterase): found in erythrocyte membranes, nervous tissue, skeletal muscle
  • Plasma cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase/butyrylcholinesterase): found in serum, liver, pancreas, heart, brain

Inhibition Mechanism

  • Organophosphates bind through phosphorylation to the enzyme active site, leading to:
  • Acetylcholine accumulation at nerve synapses and neuromuscular junctions
  • Overstimulation of acetylcholine receptors (muscarinic, nicotinic, CNS)
  • Initial overstimulation followed by paralysis of cholinergic transmission
  • Cholinergic crisis with central and peripheral toxidrome

Aging Process (Critical Concept)

  • Irreversible binding of organophosphorus compound to cholinesterase through phosphorylation
  • Once aged, enzymatic activity permanently destroyed
  • Time to aging HIGHLY VARIABLE among different agents: minutes to >24 hours - Soman ages within minutes - Malathion ages within 40+ hours
  • After aging, new enzyme must be resynthesized over WEEKS for clinical recovery
  • Antidotes MUCH MORE EFFECTIVE if given BEFORE aging occurs
  • Once aged, pralidoxime cannot reactivate enzyme

Four Clinical Syndromes Following Organophosphate Exposure

  • 1. Acute poisoning (hours to days)
  • 2. Intermediate syndrome (1-5 days)
  • 3. Chronic toxicity (weeks to months from occupational exposure)
  • 4. Organophosphate-induced delayed neuropathy (weeks to months)

Acute Poisoning Timeline

  • Most poisoned patients symptomatic within first 8 hours
  • Nearly all symptomatic within 24 hours
  • Time to symptom onset varies by route: inhalation fastest, transdermal slowest
  • Dermatitis/skin irritation from agents like malathion may hasten absorption

Muscarinic Effects (Sludge/Dumbels Mnemonic)

S: Salivation (excessive) L: Lacrimation (excessive tearing) U: Urinary incontinence D: Defecation (uncontrolled) G: GI pain and distress E: Emesis (vomiting) Alternate mnemonic (

Dumbels)

D: Defecation U: Urination M: Miosis (pinpoint pupils) B: Bradycardia, Bronchorrhea, Bronchospasm ('Killer Bs') E: Emesis L: Lacrimation S: Salivation

Nicotinic Effects

  • Muscle fasciculations, cramps, weakness (including diaphragm)
  • Mydriasis (rare, due to sympathetic stimulation at ganglia)
  • Pallor
  • Tachycardia, hypertension
  • Respiratory muscle paralysis → ventilatory failure

CNS Effects

  • Anxiety, restlessness, emotional lability
  • Tremor, headache, dizziness
  • Confusion, delirium, hallucinations
  • Seizures, coma
  • Depression (in severe cases)

Clinical Severity Patterns

  • Mild to moderate: symptoms in various combinations
  • Severe exposures: nicotinic features observed first
  • Most severely poisoned: altered mental status, pinpoint pupils, excessive sweating, difficulty breathing
  • Death from respiratory failure (bronchorrhea + respiratory muscle paralysis + CNS depression)

The intermediate syndrome occurs 1 to 5 days after organophosphate exposure in up to 40% of patients following ingestion. Clinical features include paralysis of neck flexor muscles, muscles innervated by cranial nerves, proximal limb muscles, and respiratory muscles (may require respiratory support). Importantly, symptoms or signs of cholinergic excess are ABSENT in intermediate syndrome. Electromyography may assist diagnosis. Aggressive early antidote therapy and supportive measures may prevent or ameliorate syndrome severity. Symptoms usually resolve within 7 days.

Inline board-style check
Q3. A pesticide-exposed patient has diaphoresis, vomiting, pinpoint pupils, bronchorrhea, fasciculations, and progressive diaphragmatic weakness. Which finding is most directly responsible for impending death if treatment is delayed?
  • A. Profuse diarrhea causing hypovolemic shock
  • B. Respiratory failure from bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, CNS depression, and nicotinic muscle weakness
  • C. Isolated hypertension from nicotinic ganglionic stimulation
  • D. Delayed renal failure from paraquat-like oxidative injury
Incorrect. GI fluid loss can contribute to illness, but the immediate lethal pathway in severe OP poisoning is usually respiratory failure.
Correct. Tintinalli Table 201-2 emphasizes muscarinic bronchorrhea/bronchospasm, CNS effects, and nicotinic respiratory muscle weakness; airway and atropinization are time-critical.
Incorrect. Tachycardia or hypertension may occur from nicotinic stimulation, but it is not the dominant lethal mechanism in this stem.
Incorrect. That pattern fits paraquat herbicide toxicity, not acute cholinesterase inhibitor poisoning.

Diagnosis of Organophosphate Poisoning

Diagnosis and treatment are based on history and presence of suggestive toxidrome. Laboratory cholinesterase assays take time and have limitations; waiting for results delays potentially lifesaving therapy. A characteristic hydrocarbon or garlic-like odor may assist diagnosis. The cholinergic toxidrome may vary depending on intoxication's severity and predominance of muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS manifestations.

Plasma Butyrylcholinesterase (Pseudocholinesterase)

  • Easier to assay and more widely available
  • May be decreased up to 50% in asymptomatic patients not requiring treatment
  • Recovers in 28-42 days if pralidoxime NOT administered
  • Normal baseline highly variable among individuals
  • Poor standardization of normal ranges between laboratories

Red Cell Acetylcholinesterase (True Cholinesterase)

  • More accurate indicator of synaptic cholinesterase inhibition
  • Typically reduced to 10-20% of normal in moderate poisoning
  • Reduced to <10% in severe cases
  • Requires regeneration of red blood cells for recovery
  • Full activity may not be restored for up to 120 days after severe exposure
  • More reliable than plasma levels but harder to measure

Factors Depressing Baseline (Non-Poisoning Causes)

  • Genetic variants
  • Chronic disease states, liver dysfunction
  • Hypersensitivity reactions, infection, pregnancy
  • Low serum albumin states
  • Medications: succinylcholine, codeine, morphine
  • Neoplasms, malnutrition

Factitious Lowering Of Red Cell Acetylcholinesterase

  • Hemoglobinopathies, pernicious anemia
  • Oxalate-containing blood containers
  • Concurrent antimalarial treatment

Clinical Interpretation

  • Degree of cholinesterase inhibition necessary to produce symptoms is VARIABLE
  • Do NOT rely on enzyme levels for management decisions
  • Clinical toxidrome recognition MOST IMPORTANT for diagnosis

Routine Laboratory

Nondiagnostic but may include: - Evidence of pancreatitis (rare but reported) - Hypo- or hyperglycemia - Leukocytosis - Abnormal liver function

Cardiac

  • ECG changes: ST-segment changes, peaked T waves, atrioventricular block, QT prolongation
  • Dysrhythmias: torsades de pointes, ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation
  • Myocardial ischemia possible in early stages of severe toxicity

Radiographic

Chest radiograph may show pulmonary edema in severe cases

Electromyography

May identify and quantify acetylcholinesterase inhibition at neuromuscular junctions

Inline board-style check
Q4. A patient arrives 3 hours after suspected organophosphate ingestion. The pesticide bottle is unknown. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate?
  • A. Withhold atropine and pralidoxime until red blood cell acetylcholinesterase returns
  • B. Use clinical toxidrome and exposure history to start treatment; cholinesterase testing may support but should not delay therapy
  • C. Exclude OP poisoning if plasma butyrylcholinesterase is normal
  • D. Rely on serum organophosphate concentration to guide atropine endpoint
Incorrect. Tintinalli stresses treatment should not wait for laboratory confirmation when severe toxicity is suspected.
Correct. Diagnosis is clinical; cholinesterase assays can be useful but may be delayed, variable, or difficult to interpret.
Incorrect. Plasma butyrylcholinesterase is easier to obtain but can vary for many non-toxicologic reasons and does not safely exclude serious poisoning.
Incorrect. Serum OP levels are not the practical ED guide; endpoints are clinical, especially drying pulmonary secretions and hemodynamic improvement.

Management of Organophosphate Poisoning

Tintinalli source check

Table 201-3. Treatment for Organophosphate Poisoning

This is the management anchor for decontamination, monitoring, atropine escalation, pralidoxime, and benzodiazepines for seizures.

Rosen source check

Rosen Table 152.2. Specific Treatment Dosing

A second source for atropine and pralidoxime dose ranges.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen lists atropine 1-3 mg adult and pralidoxime 1-2 g bolus / pediatric 25-50 mg/kg over 30 min; Tintinalli gives OP-specific atropine escalation endpoints and pralidoxime 30 mg/kg then infusion. Tintinalli is more operational for ED titration.

Treatment consists of airway control, intensive respiratory support, general supportive measures, decontamination, prevention of absorption, and administration of antidotes. Death occurs in untreated patients through combination of bronchorrhea, respiratory muscle paralysis, and CNS depression. Immediate priorities following decontamination: (1) airway protection, (2) provision of ventilation, (3) reduction of bronchorrhea via adequate atropinization, (4) reversal of respiratory muscle paralysis through oxime administration. Therapy should NOT be withheld pending cholinesterase levels.

Critical For Preventing Secondary Poisoning

Protective Equipment

  • Healthcare workers must wear protective clothing
  • Neoprene or nitrile gloves (NOT latex — organophosphates penetrate latex)
  • Full-body protection recommended
  • Remove before leaving patient area

Clothing Removal And Disposal

  • Remove ALL clothes and accessories completely
  • Place in plastic bags
  • Dispose as hazardous materials
  • Never transport contaminated clothing in regular waste

Skin Decontamination

  • Immediately wash with copious amounts of mild detergent and water
  • Include scalp, hair, fingernails, skin, conjunctivae, skin folds
  • Avoid abrasion or irritation of skin (increases absorption)
  • Treat body fluids as contaminated

Water Runoff Management

  • Contain and dispose of contaminated runoff as hazardous material
  • Instruments can be decontaminated using chlorine bleach

Transport Considerations

  • Safe transport ensuring patient AND healthcare worker safety
  • NO helicopter transport due to secondary contamination risk

Initial Measures

  • Place patient on oxygen, cardiac monitor, pulse oximeter
  • 100% nonrebreather mask optimizes oxygenation in patients with excessive airway secretions/bronchospasm
  • Atropine administration should NOT be delayed if oxygen not immediately available
  • Gentle suction assists in clearing airway secretions from hypersalivation, bronchorrhea, emesis

Intubation Indications

  • Coma, seizures, respiratory failure
  • Excessive respiratory secretions, severe bronchospasm
  • Inability to protect airway from aspiration

Neuronmuscular Blockade

  • Use NONDEPOLARIZING agents (rocuronium, cisatracurium, vecuronium)
  • AVOID succinylcholine (metabolized by plasma butyrylcholinesterase)
  • Succinylcholine will cause severely prolonged paralysis in organophosphate poisoning
  • Extended paralysis may last hours despite standard intubation duration expectations

Fluid Management

Hypotension initially treated with IV boluses of isotonic crystalloid

Indications For Atropine

  • Pinpoint pupils (miosis)
  • Excessive sweating and secretions
  • Respiratory distress

Initial Dosing

  • Adults:
  • 1.2-3.0 mg IV depending on severity of symptoms
  • Severity-based dosing: higher doses for more severe presentation Children:
  • Start at 0.05 mg/kg IV
  • May escalate based on response

Dose Titration Protocol

  • Double the dose every 5 minutes until achieving adequate atropinization
  • Do NOT titrate to fixed heart rate or pupil size

Target Endpoints (Therapeutic Goals)

  • 1. Clear chest on auscultation (elimination of bronchorrhea)
  • 2. Heart rate >80 beats/min
  • 3. Systolic blood pressure >80 mm Hg

Critical Points

  • Pupillary dilatation is NOT a therapeutic endpoint
  • Tachycardia is NOT a contraindication to atropine - Tachycardia may result from hypoxia secondary to bronchorrhea - Atropine will reverse underlying hypoxia
  • Absence of anticholinergic symptoms after initial dose is CONSISTENT with organophosphate poisoning
  • IM atropine 2-6 mg when IV access not possible
  • LARGE amounts may be necessary: hundreds of milligrams in massive ingestions
  • Proactive contact with pharmacy may be needed to ensure adequate supplies

Continuation Therapy

  • Once adequate atropinization achieved:
  • Start continuous IV infusion: 10-20% per hour of initial dose required to achieve atropinization
  • Typical adult infusion rates: 0.4-4 mg/h IV
  • Adjust infusion to maintain adequate atropinization

Monitor For Atropine Toxicity

  • Absent bowel sounds
  • Hyperthermia
  • Delirium
  • Adjust infusion rate to prevent toxicity while maintaining effect

Alternate Agent

  • Glycopyrrolate: anticholinergic without CNS toxicity
  • Dosing not well-defined
  • No proven benefit compared to atropine
  • Adequate atropinization achievable without significant CNS toxicity via monitoring for signs of toxicity

Mechanism

  • Oxime compounds displace organophosphates from active site of acetylcholinesterase
  • Reactivates the enzyme
  • Reverses muscarinic, nicotinic, and CNS symptoms

Critical

Reverses muscle paralysis ONLY if given early, BEFORE aging occurs

Timing Is Critical For Efficacy

  • Give as soon as possible (ideally within minutes to hours)
  • May be given 24-48 hours after exposure (though earlier is substantially more effective)
  • Obtain blood samples for acetylcholinesterase levels BEFORE administration if possible
  • Do NOT delay pralidoxime waiting for lab results

Dosing (Who Recommendation)

  • Adults:
  • Initial bolus: 30 mg/kg IV (in normal saline)
  • Infuse over 5-10 minutes
  • Typical dose: 1-2 g IV bolus Children:
  • 30 mg/kg IV bolus
  • Up to 1 gram maximum total Continuation:
  • 8 mg/kg per hour IV infusion for 24-48 hours
  • Monitor acetylcholinesterase levels during infusion
  • Continue for 24-48 hours while monitoring levels

Efficacy Notes

  • More effective in acute than chronic intoxications
  • Despite theoretical benefit and worldwide clinical use, current evidence inadequate to show pralidoxime reduces mortality or complication rate in acute organophosphate poisoning
  • Recommended for use even later than 24-48 hours after exposure
  • NOT recommended for asymptomatic patients
  • NOT recommended for carbamate exposures with minimal symptoms

Treatment Approach

  • Airway protection
  • Supplemental oxygen
  • Atropine (may prevent or abort seizures from cholinergic overstimulation within first few minutes of exposure)
  • Benzodiazepines IV for seizure control (titrated to effect)

Important

  • Atropine may be sufficient to abort early seizures
  • Standard anticonvulsants (phenytoin) have NO role in organophosphate-induced seizures

Pulmonary edema and bronchospasm are treated with oxygen, intubation, positive-pressure ventilation, atropine, and pralidoxime. Succinylcholine, ester anesthetics, and beta-adrenergic blockers may potentiate poisoning and should be avoided. Some evidence exists for magnesium sulfate and calcium channel blockers, but they are not yet recommended for routine clinical use.

Gastric Lavage

  • No published evidence demonstrates improved outcome
  • May be beneficial within 1 hour of very large ingestion (after airway protection via intubation)
  • Should NOT delay timely administration of antidotal therapy

Activated Charcoal

  • Organophosphates bind in vitro
  • No evidence that single or multiple doses improve patient outcome

Enhanced Elimination

  • Hemodialysis: no proven value
  • Hemofiltration: no proven value
  • Hemoperfusion: no proven value
Inline board-style check
Q5. After decontamination and oxygenation, an adult with severe OP poisoning remains bronchorrheic after atropine 3 mg IV. What is the best next atropine strategy?
  • A. Repeat the same 3 mg dose every hour only
  • B. Double IV atropine every 5 minutes until chest secretions clear, then start an infusion based on the loading dose
  • C. Stop atropine when pupils dilate, because mydriasis is the therapeutic endpoint
  • D. Use pralidoxime alone because atropine worsens nicotinic weakness
Incorrect. Hourly fixed dosing is too slow for life-threatening bronchorrhea.
Correct. Tintinalli Table 201-3: double IV atropine every 5 minutes until adequate atropinization, then continue infusion at roughly 10%-20% per hour of the required loading dose.
Incorrect. Pupil size is not the endpoint. Clear lungs, improved oxygenation, HR, and blood pressure are more important.
Incorrect. Pralidoxime does not replace atropine. Atropine reverses muscarinic bronchorrhea/bronchospasm; 2-PAM helps regenerate cholinesterase before aging.

Disposition and Follow-up

  • Minimal exposures: decontamination and 6-8 hours ED observation to detect delayed effects
  • Avoid reexposure: sequential exposures result in cumulative toxicity
  • Work restrictions: patients returning to work should be limited from further exposure
  • ICU admission necessary for significant poisonings
  • Most patients respond to pralidoxime with acetylcholinesterase level increase within 48 hours
  • If treated early and no post-hypoxic brain damage: symptomatic recovery within 10 days
  • Fat-soluble toxins: patient may be symptomatic for prolonged periods, dependent on continuous pralidoxime infusion
  • Supportive care and respiratory support may be needed while awaiting enzyme resynthesis (weeks)
  • Endpoint of therapy: absence of signs and symptoms on withholding pralidoxime

Carbamates: Reversible Cholinesterase Inhibition

Carbamate insecticides include aldicarb, carbofuran, carbaryl, ethienocarb, fenobucarb, oxamyl, methomyl, pirimicarb, propoxur, and trimethacarb. These are cholinesterase inhibitors structurally related to organophosphate compounds. Primarily used as insecticides, though illegally imported rodenticides may contain aldicarb.

Carbamate Binding Mechanism

  • Transiently and reversibly bind to cholinesterase enzyme
  • Regeneration of enzyme activity by dissociation occurs within minutes to a few hours
  • Involves rapid, spontaneous hydrolysis of carbamate-cholinesterase bond
  • AGING DOES NOT OCCUR (major difference from organophosphates)
  • Restoration of normal function does NOT require generation of new enzyme

Clinical Significance

  • Cholinergic toxidrome similar to organophosphates (SLUDGE/DUMBELS)
  • Symptoms generally shorter duration than organophosphate poisoning
  • In adults: less central toxicity because carbamates less effective at penetrating CNS
  • Seizures do NOT occur in adults (unlike organophosphates)
  • In children: presentation differs with predominance of CNS depression and nicotinic effects
  • Intermediate syndrome can occur (reported in carbamate poisoning)
  • Most patients recover completely within 24 hours

Carbamates can be toxic after dermal, inhalation, and GI exposure. Although carbamate poisoning produces similar cholinergic toxidrome to organophosphate poisoning, clinical presentation may be milder and of shorter duration due to reversible nature of enzyme inhibition.

Treatment Approach

  • Decontamination (same as organophosphates)
  • Atropine (same indications and dosing as organophosphates) - Titrate to DRY secretions - Initial 2-4 mg IV, doubling every 5-10 minutes - Continue infusion 10-20% per hour of initial dose
  • Therapy usually not needed for more than 6-12 hours

Pralidoxime Use In Carbamates (Controversial)

  • Carbamate-binding half-life to cholinesterase approximately 30 minutes
  • Irreversible binding does NOT occur
  • Little need for pralidoxime (enzyme recovers naturally)
  • Some case reports and animal studies suggest pralidoxime may POTENTIATE toxicity of carbamates such as carbaryl
  • Pralidoxime generally NOT recommended or may increase toxicity
  • Atropine alone often sufficient while carbamylated acetylcholinesterase complex dissociates spontaneously

Controversy Resolution

  • Pralidoxime may be considered in severe carbamate poisonings
  • Should be avoided in known single-agent carbaryl poisonings
  • Should be considered in MIXED poisonings (organophosphorus compound + carbamate)
  • Should be considered if type of insecticide is UNKNOWN (could be organophosphate)
  • NOT indicated in carbamate exposures presenting with minimal symptoms

Pyrethroids: Sodium Channel Toxins

Pyrethrins are naturally occurring insecticides derived from chrysanthemum flowers. Pyrethroids are synthetic analogs with greater potency and environmental persistence, but considered safer than organochlorine and organophosphate insecticides. Pyrethroid use and poisonings have increased since phaseout of organophosphate insecticides for use in human dwellings.

Pyrethrins are common ingredients in over-the-counter household insecticides, pediculicides, and scabicides. They are rapidly hydrolyzed by mammals and therefore pose low risk of human toxicity. Pyrethroids are used commonly as aerosols in automated insect sprays in public areas; therefore, inhalation is the most common source of exposure.

Mechanism

  • Block sodium channel at neuronal cell membrane
  • Cause repetitive neuronal discharge
  • Inhibit γ-aminobutyric acid receptors
  • Increase nicotinic cholinergic transmission
  • Promote norepinephrine release
  • Interfere with sodium-calcium exchange across cell membranes

Toxicity Sources

  • Dermal absorption (especially from concentrated products)
  • Pulmonary inhalation (most common from aerosol sprays)
  • GI ingestion (less common)
  • Allergic hypersensitivity reactions MOST COMMON effects

Allergic Manifestations

  • Dermatitis (contact)
  • Bronchospasm
  • Rhinitis
  • Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  • Anaphylaxis
  • Pyrethrin antigens cross-antigenic with ragweed pollen

Systemic Toxicity (Uncommon)

  • Occurs from occupational poisonings and large intentional ingestions
  • Features: fatigue, lethargy, nausea/vomiting, paresthesias (especially face/extremities), tremor
  • Hyperexcitability, muscle fasciculations, pulmonary edema, respiratory failure, seizures
  • Muscle fasciculations and skin contact paresthesias characteristic
  • Paresthesias and burning occur within 30 minutes of contact, usually dissipate within 24 hours

Treatment includes removal from exposure, dermal/ocular/GI decontamination, treatment of allergic manifestations, and supportive care. Diagnosis is dependent on history of exposure. Differential diagnosis includes allergic reactions and ingestions with neurologic stimulants. Laboratory tests have no diagnostic value. Disposition usually related to severity of asthmatic and allergic manifestations. The clinical course is usually benign, and hospitalization is not necessary for most accidental exposures.

Herbicides: Paraquat, Diquat, Glyphosate, and Other Classes

Tintinalli source check

Table 201-4. Selected Herbicide Classes That Pose Potential Harm to Humans

This table frames the herbicide subsection and reminds you that chlorophenoxy compounds, bipyridyls, urea-substituted herbicides, organophosphates, and glyphosate are not interchangeable.

Herbicide toxicity varies by compound and formulation. Some products cause mainly local irritation, while bipyridyl herbicides, especially paraquat, can produce severe corrosive GI injury, renal and hepatic failure, delayed pulmonary fibrosis, refractory hypoxemia, and death.

Board anchor: paraquat is the herbicide that should make you think “caustic ingestion plus delayed progressive lung injury.” Avoid supplemental oxygen unless the patient is severely hypoxic because oxygen can worsen oxidative injury.

Paraquat / Diquat

  • Paraquat is rapidly absorbed after ingestion and concentrates in lung tissue.
  • Early symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and oral/pharyngeal ulceration.
  • Severe ingestion progresses to renal failure, hepatic injury, myocarditis, shock, pulmonary fibrosis, and refractory hypoxemia.
  • Management is early decontamination, GI consultation for corrosive injury, supportive care, and toxicology consultation; hemoperfusion may be considered early where available.
Tintinalli source check

Table 201-5. Paraquat Toxicity From Ingestion

Keep this table next to paraquat because prognosis depends strongly on amount ingested and early renal, hepatic, and pulmonary findings.

Rosen source check

Rosen Table 152.3. Differential Diagnoses for Substituted Phenol Poisoning

Use this when reviewing chlorophenoxy/substituted phenol herbicide mimics.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli does not highlight substituted phenol differential diagnosis as a table in Ch201; Rosen explicitly compares toxicologic, infectious, and environmental mimics such as salicylates, sepsis, hyperthermia, and heat stroke.

Glyphosate and Other Herbicides

  • Glyphosate products often contain surfactants; severe toxicity is more likely after large-volume ingestion of concentrated formulations.
  • Chlorophenoxy herbicides can cause mucous membrane irritation, GI symptoms, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperthermia, and dysrhythmias.
  • Urea-substituted herbicides are usually lower toxicity but may require supportive care; organophosphate herbicide poisoning is treated like OP insecticide poisoning.
Inline board-style check
Q6. A patient intentionally ingests a concentrated herbicide and develops oral ulceration, vomiting, acute kidney injury, and later progressive hypoxemia with pulmonary infiltrates. Which management principle is most important?
  • A. Give high-flow oxygen immediately to prevent pulmonary fibrosis
  • B. Treat as paraquat until proven otherwise; prioritize early decontamination/toxicology consultation and avoid supplemental oxygen unless severe hypoxemia is present
  • C. Administer atropine and pralidoxime as first-line antidotes
  • D. Discharge after 6 hours if the ECG is normal
Incorrect. Supplemental oxygen can worsen paraquat oxidative lung injury and should be avoided unless severe hypoxemia requires it.
Correct. The caustic GI injury plus delayed pulmonary fibrosis pattern is classic for paraquat; early decontamination and toxicology consultation are central.
Incorrect. Atropine/2-PAM are OP therapies, not paraquat antidotes.
Incorrect. Paraquat can progress after an initially nonspecific presentation; normal ECG does not make the ingestion low risk.

Rodenticides: Anticoagulant and Non-anticoagulant Agents

Rosen source check

Rosen Table 152.4. Rodenticides (RATS PANIC)

Rosen gives a memorable RATS PANIC table for non-anticoagulant rodenticides.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Tintinalli Table 201-6 is more comprehensive and includes treatment details across more agents; Rosen is more mnemonic and highlights disposition/diagnostic clues for the classic RATS PANIC group.
Tintinalli source check

Table 201-6. Selected Non-anticoagulant Rodenticides

This table belongs in the rodenticide section because the mechanisms and treatments differ widely; do not manage strychnine, barium, thallium, phosphides, and red squill as one generic ingestion.

Rodenticides are classified clinically into anticoagulants and non-anticoagulants. Anticoagulants range from warfarin-type agents to long-acting superwarfarins; non-anticoagulants include arsenic, barium salts, elemental phosphorus, sodium fluoroacetate, strychnine, tetramine, thallium, phosphides, cholecalciferol, and red squill.

Superwarfarin clue: INR can remain normal early after ingestion, then rise later. Recheck INR at 12, 24, and 48 hours after acute intentional ingestion; treat significant coagulopathy with vitamin K1 and bleeding support.

Key Points: Pesticide Poisoning

Cholinergic Toxidrome

  • OPs + carbamates inhibit cholinesterase → ACh accumulation.
  • Think SLUDGE/DUMBELS plus nicotinic weakness and CNS toxicity.
  • Death is usually from bronchorrhea + bronchospasm + respiratory muscle paralysis.

Aging = OP Trap

  • Organophosphates can become irreversibly bound after aging.
  • Time to aging is variable: minutes to >24 h depending on agent.
  • Pralidoxime works best before aging; give early when severe OP is suspected.

Atropine Endpoint

  • Give atropine until clear chest, improved oxygenation/perfusion, HR >80, SBP >80.
  • Do NOT use pupil size as the endpoint.
  • Tachycardia is not a reason to stop atropine if secretions persist.

2-PAM / Pralidoxime

  • Use for severe OP poisoning, nicotinic weakness, or mixed/unknown cholinesterase inhibitor exposure.
  • Adult dose anchor: 30 mg/kg IV, then infusion when indicated.
  • Do not delay for cholinesterase labs.

Carbamates

  • Binding is reversible; aging does not occur.
  • Clinical course is usually shorter than OP poisoning.
  • Pralidoxime is controversial; consider only if severe, mixed, or unknown agent.

Decontamination Safety

  • Protect staff: neoprene/nitrile gloves, not latex.
  • Remove clothes/accessories and bag as hazardous waste.
  • Wash skin/hair/nails/folds; contain runoff as hazardous material.

Airway / Paralysis

  • Intubate early for coma, seizures, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, or respiratory failure.
  • Avoid succinylcholine; use nondepolarizing paralytics.
  • Respiratory failure may persist after muscarinic signs improve.

Intermediate Syndrome

  • Occurs after apparent recovery, often 24-96 h after exposure.
  • Neck flexor, proximal limb, cranial nerve, and respiratory muscle weakness.
  • Cholinergic signs may be absent; monitor severe cases in ICU.

Paraquat

  • Caustic GI injury + renal/hepatic failure + delayed pulmonary fibrosis.
  • Avoid oxygen unless severe hypoxemia.
  • No reliable antidote; early decontamination and toxicology consultation matter.

Rodenticides

  • Superwarfarins may have delayed INR rise; recheck at 12/24/48 h after intentional ingestion.
  • Use vitamin K1 for clinically important anticoagulation.
  • Non-anticoagulants are heterogeneous: use Rosen/Tintinalli tables, not one generic algorithm.

Inline MCQs

Q1. A 42-year-old farmer is brought in after accidental spraying with an organophosphate insecticide. He has excessive lacrimation, profuse salivation, bronchospasm, and miosis. His HR is 44 and BP is 80/50. Which mechanism best explains his presentation?
  • A. Competitive antagonism of acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors
  • B. Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase causing ACh accumulation
  • C. Direct muscarinic receptor agonism without cholinesterase inhibition
  • D. Alpha-adrenergic receptor blockade causing vasodilation and bradycardia
❌ Incorrect. Organophosphates do not antagonize nicotinic receptors. They inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing ACh accumulation at BOTH muscarinic and nicotinic receptors.
✅ Correct. Organophosphates phosphorylate and irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase. The resulting ACh excess activates muscarinic receptors (SLUDGE) causing the classic cholinergic toxidrome. Nicotinic effects (muscle fasciculations, weakness) also occur.
❌ Incorrect. Organophosphates act indirectly by preventing ACh degradation, not by directly activating muscarinic receptors. This distinction is important for treatment.
❌ Incorrect. The bradycardia and hypotension in organophosphate poisoning result from excess parasympathetic (cholinergic) activity, not adrenergic blockade.
Q2. A patient with organophosphate poisoning is being treated with atropine. After 2 mg IV atropine, secretions are still copious and he remains bradycardic. What is the correct approach to atropine dosing in this situation?
  • A. Stop atropine — 2 mg is the maximum safe dose to avoid toxicity
  • B. Switch to scopolamine as it has greater central efficacy against organophosphates
  • C. Double the atropine dose every 5 minutes until secretions dry; titrate to dry secretions not pupil size
  • D. Add physostigmine to potentiate atropine's effects
❌ Incorrect. Standard doses of atropine are completely inadequate for organophosphate poisoning. Massive doses (potentially >100 mg) are required. The competing ACh excess requires far more atropine than in other settings.
❌ Incorrect. Scopolamine is not the primary treatment for organophosphate poisoning. Atropine in massive doses is the standard. Benzodiazepines address CNS effects (seizures).
✅ Correct. Atropine titration in OP poisoning uses secretion control as the endpoint. Double every 5 minutes until bronchorrhea and bronchospasm resolve. Mydriasis and tachycardia are NOT reliable endpoints and indicate neither toxicity nor success.
❌ Incorrect. Physostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase and would worsen ACh excess — it is absolutely contraindicated in organophosphate poisoning.

Thai EM Board MCQs

Q1. ผู้ป่วยชายอายุ 35 ปี ถูกส่งมาด้วยอาการชัก น้ำลายไหลมาก หลอดลมตีบ และตาเข้าม่านตาแคบ ญาติเล่าว่าผู้ป่วยดื่มยาฆ่าแมลงที่บ้าน CBC พบ WBC 12,000 ข้อใดต่อไปนี้เป็นสิ่งที่ควรให้ก่อนเป็นอันดับแรก?
  • A. Atropine IV ขนาดใหญ่ (เริ่ม 2-4 mg แล้ว double ทุก 5 นาที) จนกว่า secretions แห้ง
  • B. Activated charcoal ทางปาก 50g ทันที
  • C. Physostigmine 2 mg IV เพื่อ reverse cholinergic effects
  • D. Diazepam เพื่อแก้ชักเท่านั้น ก่อนให้ยาอื่น
✅ ถูก. Atropine เป็น first-line สำหรับ organophosphate poisoning titrate จนสารคัดหลั่งแห้ง ไม่ใช่จน pupil โต หรือ HR เร็ว
❌ ผิด. ผู้ป่วยมีอาการชักและ altered mental status ซึ่งเป็น contraindication ต่อ activated charcoal (aspiration risk)
❌ ผิด. Physostigmine ยับยั้ง acetylcholinesterase ซึ่งจะทำให้ ACh สะสมมากขึ้น — contraindicated อย่างเด็ดขาดใน organophosphate poisoning
❌ ผิด. Benzodiazepine ใช้แก้ชักได้ แต่ต้องให้ Atropine ก่อนหรือพร้อมกัน เพราะ bronchospasm และ bronchorrhea เป็น life-threatening ที่ต้องแก้ทันที
Q2. ผู้ป่วยหญิงอายุ 28 ปี ได้รับ atropine ไปแล้ว 20 mg สำหรับ organophosphate poisoning แต่ยังมี muscle fasciculations และแขนขาอ่อนแรง ข้อใดต่อไปนี้เป็นสาเหตุที่ถูกต้องที่สุด?
  • A. Atropine dose ยังไม่เพียงพอ ต้องให้เพิ่มอีก
  • B. Atropine ไม่สามารถ block nicotinic effects — ต้องให้ Pralidoxime เพื่อ reactivate cholinesterase
  • C. ผู้ป่วยเกิด 'aging' ของ cholinesterase แล้ว ทำให้รักษาไม่ได้
  • D. Carbamate จะไม่ตอบสนองต่อยาใดๆ muscle weakness จึงต้องรอหาย
❌ ผิด. Atropine ไม่สามารถ block nicotinic effects ได้ การเพิ่ม atropine จะไม่แก้ muscle weakness หรือ fasciculations
✅ ถูก. Atropine เป็น muscarinic antagonist เท่านั้น Pralidoxime (2-PAM) reactivate cholinesterase และลด ACh excess ที่ทั้ง muscarinic และ nicotinic receptors รวมถึง neuromuscular junction
❌ ผิด. Aging เป็นปัญหาสำหรับ Pralidoxime ไม่ใช่ Atropine และไม่ได้อธิบาย muscle symptoms ที่ยังคงอยู่ขณะได้ atropine เพียงพอ
❌ ผิด. Carbamates ก็ตอบสนองต่อ atropine แต่ Pralidoxime มักไม่ใช้ใน carbamate poisoning (spontaneous reactivation occurs) สำหรับ organophosphate ต้องให้ Pralidoxime เร็ว
Q3. ข้อใดต่อไปนี้เป็นความแตกต่างที่สำคัญระหว่าง carbamate และ organophosphate poisoning ในแง่ของการรักษา?
  • A. Carbamate ต้องให้ Pralidoxime ในขนาดสูงกว่า organophosphate
  • B. Atropine ใช้ได้กับ organophosphate เท่านั้น ห้ามใช้ใน carbamate
  • C. Carbamate ทำให้เกิด cholinergic crisis ที่รุนแรงกว่าและนานกว่า organophosphate
  • D. Pralidoxime ไม่จำเป็นสำหรับ carbamate เพราะ cholinesterase inhibition เป็นแบบ reversible
❌ ผิด. ตรงข้าม — Pralidoxime มักไม่จำเป็นสำหรับ carbamate เพราะ reversible inhibition ทำให้ enzyme reactivation เกิดเอง
❌ ผิด. Atropine ใช้ได้กับทั้งสองชนิด เพราะทั้งคู่เพิ่ม ACh ที่ muscarinic receptors
❌ ผิด. โดยทั่วไป carbamate toxicity มีระยะเวลาสั้นกว่าเพราะ reversible inhibition และ spontaneous reactivation
✅ ถูก. Carbamate–enzyme complex dissociates spontaneously Pralidoxime จึงไม่มีประโยชน์ชัดเจน แต่ Atropine ยังคงเป็น mainstay ของการรักษา
Q4. ผู้ป่วยชายอายุ 50 ปี รับประทาน organophosphate เพื่อฆ่าตัวตาย ได้รับ Atropine และ Pralidoxime (2-PAM) แล้ว อาการดีขึ้น แต่ 18 ชั่วโมงต่อมา เกิด proximal limb weakness และ respiratory failure อีกครั้ง ข้อใดต่อไปนี้อธิบายภาวะนี้ได้ดีที่สุด?
  • A. Rebound cholinergic crisis จาก organophosphate ที่ยังตกค้างในร่างกาย
  • B. Atropine toxicity จากการได้รับในขนาดสูง
  • C. Intermediate Syndrome จาก persistent nicotinic receptor dysfunction ที่ neuromuscular junction
  • D. Organophosphate-induced delayed neuropathy (OPIDN)
❌ ผิด. Rebound cholinergic crisis จะมี SLUDGE symptoms กลับมา IMS มีลักษณะเป็น proximal weakness โดยเฉพาะ respiratory muscles โดยไม่มี muscarinic symptoms ชัดเจน
❌ ผิด. Atropine toxicity จะทำให้เกิด anticholinergic syndrome (mydriasis, flushing, tachycardia) ไม่ใช่ proximal weakness และ respiratory failure
✅ ถูก. IMS เกิดหลัง acute phase 24-96 ชั่วโมง มี proximal weakness, respiratory muscle involvement และไม่มี muscarinic symptoms Mechanical ventilation คือการรักษาหลัก
❌ ผิด. OPIDN เกิดหลัง 2-3 สัปดาห์และเป็น distal sensorimotor neuropathy แตกต่างจาก IMS ที่เกิดเร็วกว่าและเป็น proximal weakness จาก neuromuscular junction dysfunction

InTraining Exam MCQs

Q1. A 38-year-old agricultural worker presents with miosis, copious oral secretions, muscle fasciculations, and serum cholinesterase activity of 15% of normal (normal >70%). He is intubated for respiratory failure. Atropine 8 mg IV has been given with partial resolution of secretions. Which of the following statements about pralidoxime (2-PAM) therapy is most accurate?
  • A. Pralidoxime is effective even when given 72 hours after organophosphate exposure in all cases
  • B. Early pralidoxime administration is critical because cholinesterase aging renders the enzyme-OP complex irreversible
  • C. Pralidoxime should not be given until atropine therapy is complete
  • D. Serum cholinesterase activity below 20% is a contraindication to pralidoxime
❌ Incorrect. Efficacy of pralidoxime is time-dependent. 'Aging' (irreversible phosphonylation of the enzyme-OP complex) occurs at varying rates. For most agricultural OPs, it occurs within 24-48 hours. After aging, pralidoxime cannot reactivate cholinesterase.
✅ Correct. The enzyme undergoes 'aging' (dealkylation of the OP moiety), making the bond irreversible. Time to aging varies by compound (minutes to days). Early 2-PAM is essential for successful enzyme reactivation.
❌ Incorrect. Atropine and pralidoxime are given together — they address different aspects (muscarinic vs. all receptor sites). There is no reason to delay pralidoxime pending atropine completion.
❌ Incorrect. Low cholinesterase activity is precisely the indication for pralidoxime. Severe inhibition (low activity) makes reactivation with 2-PAM more important, not contraindicated.

McGraw-Hill Specialty Board Review MCQs

Q1. A 25-year-old presents after dermal exposure to an organophosphate during crop spraying. She has miosis, diaphoresis, and HR 52. She is alert and cooperative. Serum RBC cholinesterase is 25% of normal. Which is the best initial decontamination approach?
  • A. Administer activated charcoal 50g PO immediately
  • B. Begin gastric lavage with 2L normal saline
  • C. Remove all clothing and wash skin with soap and water; staff wear PPE
  • D. Irrigate eyes with saline only; skin exposure does not require decontamination
Dermal decontamination is critical for organophosphate skin exposure to stop ongoing absorption. Remove all clothing (which may retain 80% of the agent) and wash skin thoroughly with soap and water. Healthcare providers must wear PPE (gown, gloves) to prevent secondary contamination. This should occur BEFORE or concurrent with drug therapy. Gastric lavage is not indicated for dermal exposure.
Q2. A patient with organophosphate poisoning develops refractory bronchospasm and bronchorrhea despite 50 mg of atropine. Chest auscultation reveals severe wheezing. Which agent, in addition to continued atropine, would best address the bronchospasm?
  • A. Inhaled ipratropium and nebulized albuterol as adjuncts to IV atropine
  • B. IV epinephrine 1 mg bolus for refractory bronchospasm
  • C. Morphine for sedation to reduce respiratory distress
  • D. IV aminophylline as a phosphodiesterase inhibitor
Bronchospasm from organophosphate poisoning is caused by both muscarinic excess (cholinergic-mediated bronchoconstriction) and possibly direct smooth muscle effects. Ipratropium (inhaled anticholinergic) can provide targeted bronchodilation at the airway. Pralidoxime (2-PAM) is also critical to reactivate cholinesterase. Beta-2 agonists (albuterol) may provide additional bronchodilation in refractory cases. The key is treating both the systemic cholinergic excess with IV atropine and the local airway component.
Q3. Which of the following best differentiates pyrethroid insecticide poisoning from organophosphate poisoning?
  • A. Pyrethroid poisoning causes more severe miosis than organophosphates
  • B. Both pyrethroids and organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase
  • C. Pralidoxime is effective for pyrethroid toxicity but not for organophosphates
  • D. Pyrethroids cause facial paresthesias and normal cholinesterase; organophosphates cause cholinergic toxidrome with low cholinesterase
Pyrethroids are sodium channel modifiers that cause neurotoxicity primarily through persistent neuronal depolarization. Unlike organophosphates, they do NOT inhibit cholinesterase. Key distinguishing features: pyrethroids cause paresthesias (especially facial), no significant autonomic changes, and normal cholinesterase levels. Atropine and pralidoxime are NOT effective for pyrethroid poisoning. Treatment is supportive.
Q4. A patient survives severe organophosphate poisoning treated with atropine, pralidoxime, and intubation. Three weeks after discharge, she returns with complaints of weakness and difficulty walking. Lower extremity examination shows distal sensorimotor deficits with preserved proximal strength. What is the most likely diagnosis?
  • A. Intermediate Syndrome from delayed cholinesterase reactivation
  • B. Organophosphate-Induced Delayed Neuropathy (OPIDN) affecting distal axons
  • C. Peripheral neuropathy from pralidoxime toxicity
  • D. Recurrent organophosphate exposure from workplace contact
Organophosphate-Induced Delayed Neuropathy (OPIDN) occurs 2-3 weeks after severe OP exposure. It involves distal sensorimotor axonopathy affecting long axons (legs > arms), causing distal weakness and sensory loss. The mechanism involves phosphorylation of neuropathy target esterase (NTE), distinct from cholinesterase inhibition. There is no specific treatment; recovery may be partial. OPIDN is distinct from Intermediate Syndrome (which occurs within the first week and affects proximal/respiratory muscles).

Chapter Assessment: 20 Questions

Q1. A 55-year-old farmer ingests an unknown amount of malathion (an organophosphate). He is brought in with SLUDGE symptoms. Which of the following is the MOST important initial intervention?
  • A. Activated charcoal 50g via nasogastric tube
  • B. Pralidoxime 1g IV loading dose
  • C. Airway management and IV atropine titrated to dry secretions
  • D. Gastric lavage with 2L saline
❌ Incorrect. Activated charcoal requires an intact airway. In obtunded patients with cholinergic crisis, airway protection comes first.
❌ Incorrect. While important, pralidoxime addresses nicotinic effects and cannot reverse the immediate life-threatening bronchorrhea as effectively as atropine.
✅ Correct. Bronchorrhea and bronchospasm are the primary causes of death in OP poisoning. Atropine must be given in massive doses titrated to secretion control.
❌ Incorrect. Gastric lavage is not recommended without airway protection and is not the first priority in a symptomatic patient.
Q2. Which mnemonic correctly describes the muscarinic effects of organophosphate poisoning?
  • A. MUDPILES
  • B. SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis)
  • C. AEIOU TIPS
  • D. RSVP
❌ Incorrect. MUDPILES (Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Propylene glycol, INH/Iron, Lactic acid, Ethylene glycol, Salicylates) describes the causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis, not cholinergic toxidrome.
✅ Correct. SLUDGE describes the muscarinic effects of acetylcholine excess from organophosphate poisoning. DUMBELS is the alternative mnemonic.
❌ Incorrect. AEIOU TIPS is a mnemonic for altered mental status causes (Alcohol, Epilepsy, Insulin, Opioids, Uremia, Trauma, Infection, Psychiatric, Stroke).
❌ Incorrect. Not a standard toxicology mnemonic for cholinergic effects.
Q3. A firefighter responds to a scene where workers were accidentally exposed to parathion. He assists victims without PPE and develops miosis 30 minutes later. What is the most appropriate next step for the firefighter?
  • A. Immediate decontamination: remove clothing and wash skin thoroughly with soap and water
  • B. Administer pralidoxime 1g IV immediately and continue rescue operations
  • C. Observe for 1 hour; miosis alone indicates minimal toxicity requiring no treatment
  • D. Activated charcoal PO as the agent may have been ingested during mouth breathing
✅ Correct. Ongoing dermal absorption must be stopped first. Clothing removal and skin washing are the critical first steps. PPE for treaters is essential.
❌ Incorrect. Decontamination must occur before drug therapy to prevent ongoing exposure. Continuing operations without decontamination would worsen toxicity.
❌ Incorrect. Miosis indicates significant exposure. Decontamination and evaluation are mandatory regardless of symptom severity. More severe toxicity may develop.
❌ Incorrect. The exposure was dermal. Activated charcoal is not indicated for dermal exposure.
Q4. A 10-year-old child is brought in after ingesting an organophosphate ant bait. He has mild miosis and diaphoresis but is alert with normal vital signs. RBC cholinesterase is 35% of normal. Which treatment is most appropriate?
  • A. Immediate intubation for airway protection
  • B. Atropine 2 mg IV bolus q30 min for 6 hours
  • C. Ipecac syrup for GI decontamination
  • D. Close monitoring with atropine and pralidoxime available for use if symptoms progress
❌ Incorrect. The child is alert with normal vital signs. Intubation is not indicated without impending airway compromise or respiratory failure.
❌ Incorrect. Fixed-dose atropine schedules are inappropriate. Atropine must be titrated to clinical response (secretion drying). Prophylactic fixed dosing may cause toxicity.
❌ Incorrect. Ipecac is contraindicated in organophosphate poisoning as it can accelerate absorption and may cause aspiration in patients who deteriorate rapidly.
✅ Correct. Mild OP poisoning in an alert child with normal vitals can be managed with close observation. Atropine and pralidoxime should be immediately available and given if symptoms progress.
Q5. Which of the following organophosphates is associated with the SHORTEST time to cholinesterase 'aging,' requiring the most rapid antidotal treatment?
  • A. Malathion
  • B. Soman (GD)
  • C. Chlorpyrifos
  • D. Parathion
❌ Incorrect. Malathion has a longer aging time (24-48 hours), allowing a reasonable window for pralidoxime therapy.
✅ Correct. Soman undergoes aging within minutes. By the time a victim reaches medical care, pralidoxime is largely ineffective. This makes soman (a nerve agent) extremely lethal and management relies on high-dose atropine and benzodiazepines.
❌ Incorrect. Chlorpyrifos ages over hours to days, providing a reasonable window for pralidoxime therapy.
❌ Incorrect. Parathion ages within 24-48 hours — much slower than soman.
Q6. A patient with organophosphate poisoning develops new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures after initial resuscitation. Atropine and pralidoxime are being given. Which is the most appropriate treatment for the seizures?
  • A. Phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV loading dose
  • B. Increase atropine dose to suppress seizure activity
  • C. IV benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, or midazolam)
  • D. Levetiracetam 1g IV as a non-sedating anticonvulsant option
❌ Incorrect. Phenytoin is not effective for organophosphate-induced seizures. These seizures are driven by cholinergic excess, not sodium channel dysregulation. Benzodiazepines are required.
❌ Incorrect. While atropine blocks muscarinic effects peripherally, it crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly. It does not reliably suppress central cholinergic-mediated seizures.
✅ Correct. Benzodiazepines are first-line for OP seizures. They enhance GABA-ergic inhibition to counteract the cholinergic CNS excitation. High doses may be required.
❌ Incorrect. Levetiracetam has no established role in organophosphate-induced seizures. Benzodiazepines are the standard of care.
Q7. A 32-year-old woman presents after ingesting a 'natural' insecticide containing pyrethrin (a pyrethroid). She has severe pruritus, facial tingling, and paresthesias over her arms. Vital signs are normal. Which statement about her management is most accurate?
  • A. Atropine and pralidoxime are indicated to reverse cholinesterase inhibition
  • B. Measure RBC cholinesterase activity to guide treatment intensity
  • C. High-dose atropine should be given to block sodium channel effects
  • D. Treatment is supportive; vitamin E oil may relieve skin paresthesias; atropine is not indicated
❌ Incorrect. Pyrethroids do not inhibit cholinesterase. Atropine and pralidoxime have no role in pyrethroid toxicity.
❌ Incorrect. Cholinesterase is not inhibited by pyrethroids. Cholinesterase levels are not a useful biomarker for pyrethroid poisoning.
❌ Incorrect. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, not sodium channels. It would have no effect on pyrethroid-induced sodium channel dysfunction.
✅ Correct. Pyrethroid management is supportive. Skin paresthesias may be relieved by topical vitamin E oil. Systemic seizures are treated with benzodiazepines if they occur. Cholinergic antidotes are not needed.
Q8. Which laboratory test is most useful for confirming organophosphate poisoning and monitoring treatment response?
  • A. RBC (erythrocyte) cholinesterase activity
  • B. Plasma cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase)
  • C. Serum creatinine kinase (CK)
  • D. Urine drug screen for organophosphate metabolites
✅ Correct. RBC cholinesterase is the more specific marker for OP poisoning and correlates with synaptic enzyme inhibition. It is the preferred test for confirming diagnosis and monitoring recovery.
❌ Partially correct — plasma cholinesterase is measurable and does decrease in OP poisoning, but it is less specific (also reduced in liver disease, malnutrition). RBC cholinesterase is preferred.
❌ Incorrect. CK reflects muscle breakdown and may be elevated with severe fasciculations, but it is not a specific marker for OP poisoning or a guide for treatment.
❌ Incorrect. Standard urine drug screens do not test for organophosphate metabolites. Specific metabolite testing (e.g., urinary alkyl phosphates) exists but is not widely available and not used clinically for treatment guidance.
Q9. A patient is referred with carbamate (aldicarb) poisoning. The treating physician is considering whether to give pralidoxime. What is the most appropriate recommendation?
  • A. Give pralidoxime immediately — it is always indicated for cholinesterase inhibitor poisoning
  • B. Pralidoxime is not routinely recommended for carbamate poisoning; atropine is the primary treatment
  • C. Pralidoxime is contraindicated for carbamate but indicated for organophosphate — do not give
  • D. Carbamate poisoning does not respond to any antidotes; only supportive care is possible
❌ Incorrect. Pralidoxime is indicated for organophosphates but NOT routinely recommended for carbamates due to spontaneous reactivation and possible adverse interaction.
✅ Correct. Carbamate inhibition is reversible and spontaneous reactivation occurs. Atropine titrated to secretion control is the mainstay. Pralidoxime is controversial and not routinely given.
❌ Partially correct — pralidoxime is not indicated, but 'contraindicated' overstates the evidence. The correct term is 'not routinely recommended.'
❌ Incorrect. Atropine is highly effective for carbamate poisoning to block muscarinic effects. Supportive care is important, but antidotal therapy with atropine is standard.
Q10. An outdoor worker applies a concentrated pyrethroid insecticide spray and develops sudden onset confusion, ataxia, and clonic limb movements 2 hours later. Vital signs: HR 100, BP 120/80, SpO2 96%. No miosis. No excessive secretions. What is the most appropriate management?
  • A. Atropine 4 mg IV followed by pralidoxime 1g IV
  • B. Physostigmine 2 mg IV to reverse central anticholinergic effects
  • C. Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV to reverse possible benzodiazepine ingestion
  • D. Supportive care with benzodiazepines for seizure control; decontaminate skin
❌ Incorrect. Pyrethroids do not inhibit cholinesterase. The absence of cholinergic signs (no miosis, no secretions) and the presence of CNS excitation confirms this is not organophosphate poisoning.
❌ Incorrect. Physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxidrome. This patient does not have anticholinergic signs (would expect mydriasis, dry skin, tachycardia, urinary retention). Pyrethroid toxicity is a different mechanism.
❌ Incorrect. There is no history of benzodiazepine use, and flumazenil is contraindicated when seizures are possible (can precipitate refractory status epilepticus in benzo-dependent patients).
✅ Correct. Pyrethroid toxicity is managed supportively. Benzodiazepines control seizures. Skin decontamination stops ongoing absorption. No cholinergic antidotes needed.
Q11. What is the key principle that determines the correct atropine titration endpoint in severe organophosphate poisoning?
  • A. Tachycardia (HR >100 bpm)
  • B. Pupil dilation to >5 mm
  • C. Cessation of bronchorrhea and resolution of bronchospasm
  • D. Correction of miosis to normal pupil size
❌ Incorrect. Tachycardia is an early atropine effect and occurs before secretions dry. Using tachycardia as the endpoint results in undertreating the life-threatening bronchorrhea/bronchospasm.
❌ Incorrect. Mydriasis is an early and unreliable endpoint. It may occur before secretions are adequately controlled, leading to premature cessation of dosing.
✅ Correct. The life-threatening manifestations of OP poisoning are bronchorrhea and bronchospasm. Atropine must be given until these resolve, regardless of what the pulse or pupils are doing.
❌ Incorrect. Miosis may persist for days even with adequate atropine treatment because of persistent ACh activity at ciliary muscle receptors. It is not a reliable endpoint for systemic atropine therapy.
Q12. A man is found unresponsive near agricultural fields. He has miosis, copious salivation, bradycardia of 38, and urinary incontinence. He is intubated for airway protection. Which of the following is an expected finding on ECG?
  • A. Right bundle branch block (RBBB)
  • B. Prolonged PR interval and QTc prolongation
  • C. ST elevation in V1-V4 consistent with anterior STEMI
  • D. Delta waves suggesting Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
❌ Incorrect. RBBB is not specifically associated with organophosphate poisoning. The cardiac effects are primarily vagotonic — bradycardia and conduction delays.
✅ Correct. Excess vagal tone from ACh accumulation causes PR prolongation and may cause complete heart block. QTc prolongation occurs and can predispose to Torsades de Pointes. Bradycardia is the most common cardiac finding.
❌ Incorrect. While ischemic ECG changes can occur, STEMI pattern is not a specific or expected finding. Conduction abnormalities from vagal excess are more characteristic.
❌ Incorrect. Delta waves indicate pre-excitation and are not caused by organophosphate poisoning. They are a pre-existing condition.
Q13. A researcher describes two groups of patients with cholinesterase inhibitor poisoning: Group A had a 'reversible' enzyme complex that hydrolyzed within 4 hours; Group B had an 'irreversible' enzyme complex requiring reactivation therapy. What agents caused each group's poisoning?
  • A. Group A: carbamate; Group B: organophosphate
  • B. Group A: organophosphate; Group B: carbamate
  • C. Group A: pyrethroid; Group B: organophosphate
  • D. Group A: carbamate; Group B: pyrethroid
✅ Correct. Carbamates → reversible inhibition (spontaneous hydrolysis). Organophosphates → irreversible inhibition (requires pralidoxime for reactivation). This determines whether 2-PAM is needed.
❌ Incorrect. This is reversed. Organophosphates cause irreversible inhibition requiring pralidoxime; carbamates cause reversible inhibition.
❌ Incorrect. Pyrethroids do not inhibit cholinesterase at all. They act on sodium channels.
❌ Incorrect. Pyrethroids are not cholinesterase inhibitors. Group B must be an organophosphate.
Q14. A patient with organophosphate poisoning requires repeated atropine boluses due to recurrent bronchorrhea. The treating team wants to switch to a continuous infusion. What is the recommended infusion rate after adequate atropinization?
  • A. 1-2 mg/hour as a fixed rate regardless of initial loading dose
  • B. 10-20% of the total atropinization dose per hour, titrated to clinical response
  • C. 0.02 mg/kg/hour as a standard pediatric-derived formula
  • D. Atropine infusions are contraindicated; only bolus dosing should be used
❌ Incorrect. A fixed rate based on standard doses is inadequate. The infusion should be based on the actual loading dose required, which in severe OP poisoning may be tens of milligrams.
✅ Correct. The infusion rate is calculated from the total dose required for initial atropinization (usually 10-20% per hour). Clinical reassessment guides dose adjustments — more if secretions recur, less if anticholinergic signs appear.
❌ Incorrect. While weight-based dosing is used in pediatrics, the infusion rate must be guided by the actual loading dose and clinical response, not a standard formula.
❌ Incorrect. Continuous infusion is the preferred approach after initial atropinization to maintain effect without repeated boluses causing fluctuating drug levels.
Q15. A patient presents with a cholinergic toxidrome after exposure to a nerve agent during a terrorist attack. Atropine is given but has been insufficient for bronchospasm. Military medical kits include 'MARK-1' autoinjectors. What does the MARK-1 kit contain?
  • A. Atropine 1 mg + diazepam 5 mg
  • B. Pralidoxime 1g + glycopyrrolate 1 mg
  • C. Atropine 2 mg + pralidoxime chloride (2-PAM Cl) 600 mg
  • D. Sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq + calcium gluconate 1g
❌ Incorrect. CANA (Convulsant Antidote for Nerve Agents) contains diazepam for seizures, but MARK-1 contains atropine + pralidoxime, not diazepam.
❌ Incorrect. Glycopyrrolate is not part of MARK-1. MARK-1 contains atropine (not glycopyrrolate) + pralidoxime.
✅ Correct. MARK-1 contains atropine 2 mg + pralidoxime 600 mg in separate autoinjectors for combined muscarinic blockade and cholinesterase reactivation. Up to 3 kits may be given.
❌ Incorrect. These are used for other toxicologic emergencies (cardiac toxicity, HF poisoning). Not part of nerve agent antidote kits.
Q16. Which of the following mechanisms correctly describes how organophosphates exert their toxic effects at the nicotinic neuromuscular junction?
  • A. Competitive inhibition of nicotinic receptors causing flaccid paralysis
  • B. Direct calcium channel blockade at the neuromuscular junction
  • C. Muscarinic receptor agonism causing skeletal muscle spasm
  • D. ACh excess causes initial fasciculations, then depolarization blockade leading to weakness
❌ Incorrect. OPs do not competitively block nicotinic receptors. They increase ACh (an agonist) at these receptors, initially causing excessive stimulation before depolarization block.
❌ Incorrect. OPs do not directly block calcium channels. The mechanism is cholinesterase inhibition leading to ACh accumulation.
❌ Incorrect. Skeletal muscle neuromuscular junctions use nicotinic receptors, not muscarinic receptors. Muscarinic effects are in smooth muscle and glands.
✅ Correct. Excess ACh at NMJ initially produces fasciculations. Prolonged ACh excess causes persistent depolarization, desensitization, and depolarization blockade — clinically manifest as weakness and paralysis. This is not reversed by atropine.
Q17. A mother brings her 2-year-old son who ate pyrethroid-containing ant powder 20 minutes ago. He is alert, playing, and asymptomatic. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
  • A. Administer atropine 0.02 mg/kg IV to prevent delayed cholinergic toxicity
  • B. Observation; consider activated charcoal if recent significant ingestion with intact airway
  • C. Gastric lavage with orogastric tube
  • D. Admit to ICU for cardiac monitoring for 48 hours
❌ Incorrect. Pyrethroids do not cause cholinergic toxicity. Atropine is not indicated.
✅ Correct. Asymptomatic pyrethroid ingestion is managed with observation. Activated charcoal may reduce absorption if given early with intact airway. No antidote is needed.
❌ Incorrect. Gastric lavage is not indicated in an asymptomatic child with a small ingestion. Risks of lavage (aspiration, trauma) outweigh benefits.
❌ Incorrect. ICU admission is not warranted for an asymptomatic 2-year-old with small pyrethroid ingestion. Observation in an appropriate clinical setting is sufficient.
Q18. In organophosphate poisoning, which of the following statements about succinylcholine is most important to communicate to the anesthesiologist managing a patient requiring intubation?
  • A. Succinylcholine is contraindicated — plasma cholinesterase is inhibited causing prolonged paralysis
  • B. Succinylcholine dose must be tripled due to cholinergic receptor resistance
  • C. Succinylcholine is safe; plasma cholinesterase is unaffected in OP poisoning
  • D. Succinylcholine and rocuronium are equally safe — use whichever is available
✅ Correct. Succinylcholine requires plasma cholinesterase for metabolism. OP-inhibited plasma cholinesterase will cause unpredictable, prolonged paralysis. Rocuronium is the preferred agent for RSI.
❌ Incorrect. There is no receptor resistance. The problem is slowed metabolism, not reduced receptor sensitivity. Increasing the dose would worsen the problem.
❌ Incorrect. Plasma cholinesterase IS inhibited in OP poisoning. Using succinylcholine risks prolonged paralysis.
❌ Incorrect. Succinylcholine is specifically problematic in OP poisoning. Rocuronium is the preferred RSI agent.
Q19. A patient exposed to an unknown organophosphate is being treated. The team notes that despite adequate atropinization, the patient has a low-grade fever and remains diaphoretic. How should these findings be interpreted?
  • A. These indicate inadequate atropinization — increase atropine dose immediately
  • B. Fever indicates secondary infection — start empiric antibiotics
  • C. Diaphoresis is a nicotinic effect not blocked by atropine — continue current atropine dosing focused on secretion control
  • D. These findings suggest the diagnosis is incorrect — reconsider alternate toxidrome
❌ Incorrect. Diaphoresis is mediated by nicotinic (sympathetic) receptors, not muscarinic. Increasing atropine will not address diaphoresis and risks atropine toxicity if secretions are already controlled.
❌ Incorrect. Low-grade fever in this context results from the hyperadrenergic/cholinergic excess state. Empiric antibiotics should not be started without clinical evidence of infection.
✅ Correct. Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors only. Nicotinic effects (diaphoresis, fasciculations, tachycardia from ganglionic stimulation) are not reversed by atropine. Pralidoxime addresses nicotinic ACh excess.
❌ Incorrect. Diaphoresis in organophosphate poisoning is expected and does not require changing the diagnosis. It reflects nicotinic excess coexisting with muscarinic effects.
Q20. A farm worker presents with organophosphate poisoning after malathion exposure. Atropine and pralidoxime are ordered. The pharmacist asks about the pralidoxime infusion rate after a 1g loading dose over 15 minutes. What is the appropriate maintenance infusion?
  • A. 100 mg/hour for 2 hours then stop
  • B. 500 mg/hour (approximately 8 mg/kg/hour) continued until clinical resolution
  • C. 2g/hour indefinitely until cholinesterase activity normalizes
  • D. Pralidoxime infusion is only needed if atropine alone fails after 4 hours
❌ Incorrect. This dose and duration are insufficient. Pralidoxime should run at 500 mg/hour and continue well beyond 2 hours based on clinical recovery.
✅ Correct. Standard pralidoxime maintenance is 500 mg/hour in adults after a 1-2g loading dose. It should continue until there is clear clinical improvement (resolution of nicotinic and muscarinic signs) and no need for further atropine.
❌ Incorrect. 2g/hour exceeds standard dosing and risks pralidoxime toxicity (dizziness, blurred vision, tachycardia, hypertension). 500 mg/hour is the standard maintenance rate.
❌ Incorrect. Pralidoxime should be started immediately alongside atropine — waiting 4 hours risks cholinesterase aging and loss of efficacy. Early administration is critical.
